name: Hepatitis B core antibody, total (anti-HBc)
summary: Total anti-HBc detects antibodies (both IgM and IgG) the immune system makes against the hepatitis B virus (HBV) core antigen. Its presence is a durable marker of natural HBV exposure — past or present — and, unlike anti-HBs, it is not produced by hepatitis B vaccination.
whatItMeans: A non-reactive (negative) result generally means no evidence of prior natural HBV infection. A reactive (positive) result indicates the person has been exposed to HBV at some point; because total anti-HBc (IgM + IgG) persists for life, it cannot by itself tell current from resolved infection and must be read alongside HBsAg and anti-HBs. Key patterns: reactive anti-HBc with reactive HBsAg suggests current infection (acute or chronic); reactive anti-HBc with reactive anti-HBs and negative HBsAg suggests past, resolved and immune infection; an isolated reactive anti-HBc (HBsAg and anti-HBs both negative) may reflect resolved infection with waning anti-HBs, a false positive, the window period, or occult infection, and often needs further testing. Crucially, because HBV vaccine contains only surface antigen, anti-HBc stays negative after vaccination — so it distinguishes natural exposure from vaccine-induced immunity (which shows only anti-HBs). This is educational information, not a diagnosis; results should be interpreted with a clinician using the full HBV panel.
confounders: Isolated anti-HBc (reactive anti-HBc with negative HBsAg and anti-HBs) has several causes — resolved infection with waning anti-HBs, false positive, window period, or occult infection — and usually needs additional testing
Window period soon after exposure: total anti-HBc may still be non-reactive despite recent infection (IgM anti-HBc rises first)
Assay differences and rare false-positive/false-negative results that require confirmatory testing
Immunocompromised or immunosuppressed states can blunt or delay antibody formation
